verdict.reasoning: Patient reports “terrible headaches since midday on the left side… I just feel like I need to vomit” and later states “Yeah, I vomited twice,” indicating left-sided headache since midday with nausea and two episodes of vomiting.
Doctor confirms timing and onset: “it started at midday a few hours ago?” (patient: “Yeah.”) and patient says the pain “just happened,” indicating sudden onset a few hours prior.
Patient: “it’s throbbing on that left side” and “if I lean forward or like move my head or neck… the headache gets worse,” confirming throbbing, left-sided, worse with leaning and neck movement.

Patient: “I noticed some zigzag lines in my vision. A few minutes before the headache started, my vision blurred,” supporting transient zigzag visual lines minutes before onset (visual aura description).
Doctor: “your vision has been blurry as well, is that right? Is that on both eyes or just a left eye?” Patient: “It feels like it’s on both,” confirming blurred vision in both eyes.
Doctor asks about bright lights; patient: “Yeah, well, I’m wearing sunglasses right now. You know, light’s really hurting my eyes,” indicating photophobia and use of sunglasses.
Initially patient: “I just feel like I need to vomit,” later confirms “Yeah, I vomited twice,” so headache is associated with nausea and two vomiting episodes.
Doctor: “Any temperatures or fevers?” Patient: “No, I don’t feel feverish,” confirming denial of fever.
Doctor: “Any other funny skin rashes that you may have noticed?” Patient: “No, I haven’t noticed anything like that,” confirming denial of rash.

Patient: “I did have a similar headache a few weeks ago.” Doctor: “How long did it last?” Patient: “For a couple of days… had to take painkillers and had to go to bed and rest,” confirming similar headache weeks ago, ~2 days, relieved with analgesia and rest.
Doctor asks about “problems with your speech… arms and legs… numbness or weakness… difficulty with balance, your balance or coordination?” Patient answers “No” to each, confirming denials.
Doctor: “have you had a fall recently or been knocked on the head?” Patient: “No,” indicating no recent head injury.
Doctor: “Do you have any other medical history I should be aware of?” Patient: “No,” indicating no reported past medical history.
Patient: “I take the pill, microgynon.” Doctor: “And how long have you been on that for?” Patient: “Three months… It’s for contraception,” matching content.
Patient: “My mum had. Has migraines, but I’ve not been diagnosed,” confirming maternal history of migraines.
Patient: “My mum has an underactive thyroid as well,” confirming maternal underactive thyroid.
Doctor: “Who’s at home with you?” Patient: “I live on my own,” confirming she lives alone.

Patient: “working fashion industry” and “Yeah, it’s really stressful, actually. Having problems with like people at work… managers… putting a lot of pressure,” confirming fashion industry job with high stress.
Doctor: “Do you smoke at all?” Patient: “No,” confirming non-smoker.
Doctor: “do you drink much in the way of alcohol?” Patient: “No,” supporting minimal or no alcohol use.
Doctor: “Do you do much in the way of exercise?” Patient: “No,” indicating little exercise.

Doctor: “I wonder whether you may… have a migraine. Migraine type headache. It sounds very classical… The headache on one side, throbbing nature, the nausea, vomiting, sensitive to bright lights.” Prior similar episode noted: “this is the second migraine you’ve had in the space of a month.” Visual aura is described earlier. This supports probable migraine with aura based on listed features.

Doctor: “I’m reassured that you don’t have anything more serious, such as meningitis or indeed brain cancer,” and earlier ROS shows no focal deficits; this matches reassurance that these are low likelihood based on history and absence of focal signs.
Doctor: “Some strong painkillers would be advisable. So, you know, think about paracetamol or even cocodamol,” confirming acute treatment plan with these analgesics.
Doctor: “and some anti inflammatories such as ibuprofen and naproxen,” confirming consideration of NSAIDs for acute treatment.
Doctor: “I think keeping a headache diary will be quite important to see exactly what’s triggering these headaches,” advising a headache diary.

Doctor: “if your headaches were to become more persistent, then we can maybe think about giving you some medications that will stop your headaches from happening in the first place. Something prophylactic medicines,” indicating future consideration of prophylactic migraine therapy if recurrent/persistent.

Doctor: “if your symptoms aren’t getting better in the next two, three days, or indeed they’re getting worse, I’d like you to come back… So if your headache’s getting worse… or your neck pain is getting worse, or you develop any weakness in your arms and legs or your vision, then I want you to come back,” matching safety-net advice as described.

Doctor: “we can have a discussion next time I see you next week, perhaps” and later mentions “prophylactic medicines” and that the pill “is something we may have a little discussion about today as well,” supporting plan for review next week with potential discussion of prophylaxis and pill implications.
